entry.title: I want a website that…
entry.content:
No admin area to learn. Open the page you want to change, click a block and edit it where it sits. Move it, swap it for another block, or open its settings beside it.

Every block is tested for contrast, keyboard use and screen readers before it ships.

"Future" Traveler helps you find everything you can do. One search box runs the whole site: look for the glowing goggles, labelled Search and commands. Type what you are after, or say "Ok Future": a new page, a file to upload, a setting to change. Drop a Word file on it and Future offers to turn it into pages.

Start from a template, from scratch or from an import. Come back to any site in one click. The same dashboard runs on your laptop, your server, or a campus with hundreds of sites.

Remix this site

Same pages, a different look. Pick a theme, a palette or a design system and the whole site changes while you watch. This site's own look is first in the list, and one button puts it back.

Who it's for

Ten kinds of people ask "why is this for me". Here are four of them.

Build course sites and open textbooks that outlive the LMS. Import a Canvas export, get accessible, print-friendly pages people can find, and keep the content when the contract changes.

A portfolio you take with you after graduation, and a real project to build your skills on. HAX Lab students ship work that every HAX site uses.

Ship a standard web component once and it becomes an authorable block in every HAX site. No framework lock-in, and the design system comes with it.

entry.title: 7 pillars
entry.content:
HAX is the open web, built from plain text and blocks that anyone can edit. Each block is a web component.

Same blocks, same editor, which reads each component's schema. Run it as a single site, multisite or multi-tenant, or publish plain static files.

The magic script loads each element once. Later pages only fetch what is new, so every follow-up request is faster.

Seven community pillars hold it up for students, designers, educators, developers and AI agents: accessible, extensible, free and open, efficient, platform agnostic, remixable and sustainable.

So what will you launch? A docs site, a portfolio, a website, a blog, a course. Everyone gets a rocket, and our pillars are your engines of change!

Everything HAX makes meets accessibility standards by default, so authors don't need to be experts to publish work everyone can use. Blocks are tested for contrast, keyboard use and screen readers before they ship, and meaning never depends on color alone. HAX also reaches a global audience, with an interface in over 100 languages. And since you don't need to know what the web is to use it, anyone can contribute.

Authors build sites in minutes, not weeks, and agents can handle the repetitive work. Pages load only what they need, so they're fast on any connection or device. The less time we spend waiting and trying to figure out how to use something, the more time we spend dreaming the future together.

Every block and theme in HAX is a web component, so new ones follow the same rules as the ones we ship. Plugins add choices and integrations without changing the core. And because HAX can understand any block's settings, anything you build works in the editor right away.

HAX is free, open source under Apache 2.0, and built on open standards like web components, OpenAPI, WCAG and xAPI instead of a proprietary framework. Your site is plain HTML files you can take anywhere, with no lock-in and no subscription. What you make is yours to keep, change, share or move, however you see fit.

Bring content in from Word, PDFs, old sites or other CMSs, and HAX turns it into clean web pages. Those pages work on phones, tablets, laptops and big screens, in light or dark mode. Run it on PHP, Node, the command line, the desktop app, or as a static site with no server at all.

Every page is made of blocks you can rearrange, reuse or pull into another site. Bring in PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML or Markdown, and export to PDF, EPUB and other open formats. Change the theme any time and your content comes along untouched, and anything an agent makes stays fully editable by a person.

Nearly every site built since 2020 still works today, and new features reach old sites through upgrades, without rebuilds. Sites are small, load only what they need, and can run as static files, which saves energy on every visit. And the project is built to outlast any one person, with its knowledge recorded so the community can carry it forward.

Why they matter

A pillar is a promise you can check. Each one turns a value into a yes or no question that a student in their first week, a maintainer reviewing a change and an agent working alone will all answer the same way.

What each one rules out

  • Accessible. A block that cannot be used from the keyboard, or that loses contrast in dark mode, does not ship. Contrast is checked in light and dark on every change.
  • Efficient. A page does not load code it never uses. There is no build step to wait on, and the magic script fetches only the blocks a page has.
  • Extensible. Adding a block never means changing the editor. A block describes itself, and the editor reads that description.
  • Free and open. Nothing locks your content in or asks for an account to get it out. One Apache-2.0 license covers the whole stack.
  • Platform agnostic. A site is not tied to one server. The same folder runs on PHP, on Node, or as plain static files.
  • Remixable. Content is not welded to its design. Lift a page, a block or a whole site into another one and it still works.
  • Sustainable. Nothing depends on one person or one vendor. Sites made in 2020 still open today, and each term a new group of students learns to keep it that way.

Who leans on them

  • Students use them to judge their own work before anyone reviews it.
  • Maintainers use them to say yes or no to a change without it being personal.
  • Agents get them as written rules, so the work they hand back already fits.
  • Decision makers get a short list they can hold the project to, year after year.

When two pillars pull against each other, the question is which choice leaves HAX usable by more people in more places. That is ubiquity, and it is why it sits in the middle.

entry.title: The story button
entry.content:
What it is

A claim is easier to believe when you can see where it came from. This button sits beside a number, a pillar, a person or a block, and takes you straight to that story on hax.cloud. Same mark, same words, on every site.

On any HAX site

It is a block. Give it the story's address on hax.cloud. The address never changes, even when the story is renamed.

Use the small one inside a sentence or a list.

In a GitHub README

A README cannot run a block, so there it is a badge that links to the same story.

In the block gallery

Every block in the gallery gets one, so you can go from its documentation to the pillars and stories it belongs to.

The same chip for the rest of the network

HAX is more than one site, and each has its own mark. Set where the chip goes and it wears that mark, so people learn which tool they are about to open.

Each story on hax.cloud has its own address (hax.cloud/stories/ee450a19), and a whole web keeps a readable path (hax.cloud/hax-lab).

How mature is the project behind it?

Here is every platform on this page put through the same review on November 18, 2026, highest first. Pick a column heading to sort by it. HAX, Ghost and Astro are tied on points, one behind WordPress.

The findings, project by project

Open any project to read all 47 answers and what each one rests on.

Legal & Licensing

  • ✅ 5 of 5. The project is distributed with a clearly identified Open Source Initiative (OSI) Approved Open Source License ®. core/LICENSE.txt: GPL v2
  • ✅ 4 of 5. Every repository and distributed artifact includes license and copyright notices. core/COPYRIGHT.txt: copyright statement plus notices for bundled works
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project documents third-party dependencies and their licenses. core/COPYRIGHT.txt lists bundled third-party works (CKEditor5, jQuery, htmx and others) with their notices
  • 🟡 1 of 5. The project has a documented contributor licensing or contribution agreement policy. core/COPYRIGHT.txt says code is copyright the original authors under GPL; no CLA or DCO found in the repo.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project explains trademark, name, logo, and brand usage expectations. README.md: links the Drupal trademark and logo policy

Governance & Decision-Making

  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project has a public governance model describing roles, authority, and decision-making processes. https://project.pages.drupalcode.org/governance/core/drupal-core/ : roles, peer review, consensus among committers
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project records significant technical and community decisions in public venues. README.md: change records for every notable change since 2011
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project has a defined process for adding, reviewing, and removing maintainers or committers. core/MAINTAINERS.txt: active maintainers incl. provisional ones; past maintainers listed at drupal.org/core/maintainers/past
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project has policies for conflicts of interest, vendor participation, and institutional influence. An open governance issue on commercialisation shows the policy is incomplete.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project periodically reviews governance effectiveness and updates policies. drupal.org Drupal Community Governance issue queue has active items updated within the last months
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project documents and practices a standard voting procedure for decisions requiring formal approval. No written voting procedure for project decisions.
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project has an adopted, documented process for resolving community or governance disputes. https://drupal.org/conflict-resolution : Conflict Resolution Policy with escalation steps

Community Engagement

  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project identifies its target users, contributors, adopters, and stakeholder communities. README.md and drupal.org/contribute name audiences and roles
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project provides welcoming contribution pathways for non-code and code contributors. README.md: every issue gets a community fork
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project has public communication channels with clear participation norms. README.md: Drupal community and support pages; issue etiquette doc linked from SECURITY.md
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project has a code of conduct and an incident response process. https://drupal.org/dcoc : Code of Conduct revised July 1, 2023, incident report form, Conflict Resolution Team
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project measures and responds to community health indicators. Drupal Association 2025 Impact Report: 29,823 improvements from 8,819 contributors

Documentation & Onboarding

  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project has clear installation, configuration, and upgrade documentation. core/INSTALL.txt (requirements: PHP 8.5.0 or greater)
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project provides end-user documentation appropriate to its primary audiences. User guide not reviewed page by page.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project documents contributor onboarding, development environment setup, and review workflows. README.md: contributing, issue forks and merge requests
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project maintains architecture and integration documentation. core/modules/*/*.api.php API docs (e.g. core/modules/jsonapi/jsonapi.api.php)
  • ✅ 4 of 5. Documentation is maintained as part of the release and contribution process. core/CHANGELOG.txt points to change records, which are required for API changes

Project Operations & Roadmap

  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project publishes a roadmap or planning process that communicates priorities and timelines. core/CHANGELOG.txt: minors every six months, patches monthly; release cycle overview linked
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project uses a public issue tracker with triage, labels, and response expectations. README.md: drupal.org issue queue; etiquette and procedures documented
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project follows a predictable release process with changelogs and versioning. core/CHANGELOG.txt release cadence
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project has defined support channels and support boundaries. README.md: Support page and over a thousand service providers
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project tracks maintainership capacity and bus factor risks. core/MAINTAINERS.txt lists maintainers per subsystem, so unmaintained areas are visible

Security & Risk Management

  • ✅ 5 of 5. The project has a documented security policy and private vulnerability reporting process. Long-running security team with public advisories; widely used as a reference.
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project uses automated testing, dependency scanning, and continuous integration. .gitlab-ci.yml: PHPStan, Nightwatch, PHPUnit, spell check
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project manages software supply chain integrity for releases. No SBOM or signing evidence in the repo.
  • 🟡 1 of 5. The project documents privacy, data handling, and compliance-relevant practices. No privacy or data-handling document found in the repo.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project has an incident response and post-incident learning process. README.md: security advisories with announcements by email and RSS

Accessibility, Standards & Interoperability

  • ✅ 5 of 5. The project follows accessibility standards and includes accessibility in testing and release review. core/tests/Drupal/Nightwatch/Tests/a11yTestDefault.js and a11yTestAdmin.js (axe checks in CI)
  • 🟡 1 of 5. The project supports relevant education technology standards and documents interoperability. No education technology standards in core; JSON:API is a general standard.
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project provides APIs, export options, or data portability mechanisms. core/modules/jsonapi
  • ✅ 5 of 5. The project supports localization, internationalization, or adaptation for diverse institutional contexts when relevant. core/modules/language and the other core multilingual modules
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project documents supported platforms, browsers, devices, and deployment environments. core/INSTALL.txt: server requirements

Adoption, Impact & Institutional Fit

  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project describes its value proposition and use cases for higher education stakeholders. README.md: use cases from personal sites to large community sites
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project provides evidence of adoption, deployments, or community use. 2025 Impact Report: 3,300 case studies, 114 certified partners, 2,426 DrupalCon attendees
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project supports evaluation, pilots, and procurement due diligence. Certified partner program
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project documents implementation services, hosting options, or support partners when available. README.md: over a thousand Drupal providers
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project collects user feedback and uses it to improve product direction. No regular user survey found.

Financial & Organizational Sustainability

  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project identifies current and needed resources for maintenance, governance, support, and growth. Association 2025 financial overview (published 4 August 2026) names Drupal.org as its largest unfunded cost
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project has a funding, membership, sponsorship, or institutional support model. https://new.drupal.org/sustaining-members : tiers from $5,000
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project has a plan for post-grant or post-founder continuity. No explicit project-lead succession plan found.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project maintains transparent infrastructure ownership and operational dependencies. Trademark and domains are held by the founder.
  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project periodically assesses sustainability risks and publishes improvement priorities. Financial overview disclosed reserves below the board minimum and a restatement

Legal & Licensing

  • ✅ 5 of 5. The project is distributed with a clearly identified Open Source Initiative (OSI) Approved Open Source License ®. src/license.txt: GPL v2 or later
  • ✅ 3 of 5. Every repository and distributed artifact includes license and copyright notices. Per-file headers are not uniform.
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project documents third-party dependencies and their licenses. No third-party notices file or SBOM found in the repo.
  • 🟡 1 of 5. The project has a documented contributor licensing or contribution agreement policy. CONTRIBUTING.md points to the Core handbook; no CLA or DCO found. Contributions are taken as GPL by convention.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project explains trademark, name, logo, and brand usage expectations. Commercial use is licensed exclusively to Automattic.

Governance & Decision-Making

  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project has a public governance model describing roles, authority, and decision-making processes. Roles are documented; how decisions are made and by whom is described as founder-led and has been publicly contested.
  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project records significant technical and community decisions in public venues. CONTRIBUTING.md: Trac is the official tracker; every PR needs a Trac ticket
  • 🟡 2 of 5. The project has a defined process for adding, reviewing, and removing maintainers or committers. Removal process not found.
  • 🟡 1 of 5. The project has policies for conflicts of interest, vendor participation, and institutional influence. Five for the Future tracks company-sponsored contributors, but no conflict-of-interest or vendor-influence policy was found.
  • 🟡 1 of 5. The project periodically reviews governance effectiveness and updates policies. A community WordPress Governance Project existed (2019) but no periodic official governance review was found.

  • ✅ 3 of 5. The project has an adopted, documented process for resolving community or governance disputes. Covers conduct disputes; no process for governance disputes.

Community Engagement

  • ✅ 4 of 5. The project provides welcoming contribution pathways for non-code and code contributors. CONTRIBUTING.md: first-time contributor guides

entry.title: Contribute
entry.content:
HAX is built in the open by students, faculty, staff and people like you. Pick the way in that fits you today.

Join the community

Ask questions, show what you made and meet the people building HAX.

Every bug, idea and plan for all of HAX lives in one queue.

Every part of HAX is open source under Apache-2.0. Fork it, fix it, send a pull request.

HAX Lab is where students and junior developers learn by shipping real HAX work.

Put on the goggles

Contributing used to start with hunting through repositories to find where something lives. The goggles skip that. Put them on and you see what the Future Traveler sees: every piece of HAX on the screen shows how it is made, who made it, and how to make it better, right where you found it.

Point at anything to see how it is made: its markup, its settings right now, and what it is built on.

Point at anything to see who made it. Follow a person and everything they built lights up, with their story on hax.cloud one click away.

Pick the piece and say what you saw: a bug, a feature you want, docs that need fixing, or something hard to use or see. It opens a ready-filled issue with a pointer to that exact piece and a screenshot.

Use HAX in your language and report wording that is wrong or still in English, in your own language.

How to put them on

  1. Open a site in the HAX editor. browser.hax.cloud works with nothing to install.
  2. Open Search and commands and run Developer mode: goggles. The goggles join the top bar.
  3. Press the goggles to put them on, then pick a lens.
  4. Reports go to the HAX issue queue, so you need a free GitHub account to send one.

Send someone straight in

Add goggles to the address of a page open in the editor and it starts with that lens on. The lenses are code (X-ray), makers, flag and translate. For Translate, add the language too, so a friend who speaks French lands ready to help:

See who built what you use

Every block carries the people who shaped it. The Makers lens and the stories on hax.cloud connect what you use today to the students, faculty and contributors who built it. When you fix something or add something new, your name joins theirs, and the next person to put on the goggles sees it.
